fields.Q1:
WHAT IS IT MADE OF?**
Large flat slabs of pale grey stone, laid in courses about 32 px tall (16 art px) and 30–42 px wide, tinted orange by the torch. Smooth-faced — you'd put a hand on something flat and cool, not on masonry with joints you could feel.
fields.Q1_WHY: Row profile down x 350–374 gives seam dips at y = 182, 216, 246, 283, 313, 347, 377 — a course every 30–36 px. Column profile across y 394–420 gives joints at x ≈ 187, 227, 265, 283, 317, 353, 375, 401, 443, 473, 509, 539, 603 — 26–42 px apart, irregular. But those seams are only a **10–20 % brightness step**, and the slab faces between them are near-flat gradients. The decisive measurement is colour: sampled normalized RGB is **1.00 / 0.72 / 0.46** on the west column, **1.00 / 0.71 / 0.45** in the corridor floor, **1.00 / 0.71 / 0.45** on the wall band, **1.00 / 0.71 / 0.44** on the room floor. Wall and ground are the **same albedo, same hue, same everything** — separated only by brightness and by texture frequency. In the dim tier the untinted colour shows: RGB (8.9, 8.9, 11.6), a neutral cold grey.
fields.Q2:
SOLID MASS, OR FLAT PATTERN?**
**Flat pattern with an outline** — with one partial exception I'll credit.

The south face at y=422 is: 163 → **four screen pixels (2 art px) of near-black, value 31** → 93. That's it. No side face, no cap, no lip, no bevel highlight on the near edge, no height offset. The wall is a lighter-toned floor region with a keyline drawn round it.

The exception: at the corridor faces (x≈376 and x≈438) there *is* a contact shadow. At y=320, going east from the west wall: 114 (wall) → 39 → 55 → 68 → 70 → 86 → 91 → 94 → plateau 95. A **~12 px (6 art px) ambient-occlusion ramp**, mirrored on the east side (94 → 72 → 79 → 59 → 48 → 36 → 104). That ramp is a real thickness cue and it is the single best-observed thing in the image. It is completely absent from the south face, where the same wall meets the same floor.
fields.Q3:
WHERE DOES THE GROUND STOP?**
At **y = 422**, running the full width except through the gap at x 377–438. Sampled at x=300: y412–421 = (163,116,74); y422–425 = **(31,22,14)**; y426 = (93,66,42). At x=340: 198 → 36 → 128. At x=470: 166 → 37 → 110.

So the whole transition is **four screen pixels**. One hard dark line, and the value on the far side drops to roughly 55 % of the near side. Nothing else changes — not hue (identical), not texture family, not scale.
fields.Q4:
WHAT IS HOLDING THIS PLACE TOGETHER?**
**NOTHING.**

I searched the lit structure for anything that reads as load-bearing or as an applied repair — a pin, a rope lashing, a driven wedge, a timber, a strap, a hide patch, a brace. There are exactly two candidate objects and neither qualifies:
- **(133–145, 385–420)** — a vertical dark bar with four short cross-strokes. Reads as a bracket or ladder-rung set. It sits at brightness 10–15 and is invisible at 1:1.
- **(565–570, 386–450)** — a plain dark vertical bar spanning the wall band and running a little past the baseline. Reads as a heavy joint, not a fitting.

Nothing spans a crack. Nothing crosses a joint. Nothing is fastened to anything. There is no part of this wall you could cut and have something fall.
fields.Q5:
BUILT, OR REPEATED?**
**Repeated**, and I can prove it exactly rather than by impression.

- A **54 × 170 px block at (71, 70) is byte-identical to the block at (583, 70)** — max channel difference **0**, offset dx = +512, dy = 0. Same slabs, same corner bevel, same soft blob, same two crack squiggles in the same pixels. Two verbatim copies of a wall strip on one screen.
- The **west column repeats itself vertically at dy = 128 px**, r = 0.89–0.93 across y 196–352. The crack sprite at (320, 300) is pixel-identical to the one at (320, 172) — I masked both and overlaid them; the entire crack body came out as exact overlap.
- One black spall/hole decal (a rectangle with a bevelled left end and a scatter of rubble specks below it) appears **seven times**: (310,138), (438,394), (182,394), (182,74), (458,230), (10,88), (644,74). Note (182,394) and (438,394) share an exact y; so do (182,74) and (644,74).
fields.Q6:
WOULD YOU BELIEVE IT SHIPPED?**
**YES.** This is at or above the floor of a lot of shipped indie roguelikes.

Genuinely good? **No — merely competent.** It is a clean, readable, correctly-lit tile render with one good AO detail. It is not good because the wall has no material identity of its own: it is the floor at a different brightness with a keyline. Nothing about it says stone-that-has-been-held-for-four-hundred-years, or administration, or anything but "dungeon wall, warm palette."
fields.Q7:
WHAT CAN YOU ACTUALLY SEE AT 1:1?**

Legible at 1:1 on the standing surfaces — three things and no more:
1. **Black crack squiggles.** Roughly 2 art px wide, jagged, 60–90 px long. These carry the entire surface.
2. **One or two black blobs** (the spall decal), when they land in the lit zone.
3. A **faint horizontal banding** — I could tell the surface was striped, but I could not count the courses or place a single joint.

Blank at 1:1: the slab faces themselves. Between the cracks, the wall is an empty tan gradient. No grain, no pitting, no tool marks, no mortar, no colour variation between adjacent slabs. If you deleted the cracks the wall would be a flat shape.

Distance dependence — yes, sharply, in three tiers:
- **within ~100 px of the figure** (the band from x≈300–520, y 390–421): everything above is visible plus a suggestion of joints.
- **~100–250 px** (x 190–300 and 520–620 on the band; the columns at y 200–390): only the cracks survive; the surface is a tone.
- **beyond ~250 px** — including the whole top band y 0–130 — the surface sits at a flat **RGB (9, 9, 12)** and shows **nothing at all**. Sampled across the full width at y=25: 7, 8, 9, 6, 7, 8, 8, 6, 7, 10. Constant. That's not falloff, that's a remembered-map tier, and at that value on a phone it is black.
fields.Q7_WHY:
Checked at 1:1, from the native-size render: **(250–500, 390–421)** the brightest wall available; **(311–377, 260–390)** west column lower half; **(438–504, 200–390)** east column; **(0–300, 390–421)** and **(500–750, 390–421)** the band's outer runs; **(0–750, 0–130)** top band.
Only found by magnifying: the **30–36 px course seams** (needed a row-mean profile to locate at all); the **26–42 px vertical joints**; the **diagonal bevel highlight** in the top-left of some slabs; the **bracket at (133–145, 385–420)**; the **bar at (565–570, 386–450)**; the **speckle rubble** under each spall decal; and the **entire slab layout and two cracks of the top band**. All of that is hunting, not seeing.
fields.Q8:
ANYTHING YOUR EYE KEEPS RETURNING TO?**
Yes. Three things, and one of them is the reason to reject.

1. **The crack squiggle.** The same jagged black vertical zigzag keeps arriving. Verified identical at **(320, 172)** and **(320, 300)**, plus a third strong hit at **(0, 428)**. Visually the same shape family also sits at ≈(200,80), (350,70), (455,60), (540,70), (620,90), (720,70), (250,395), (500,400), (600,395). It is the only damage vocabulary in the image and it is one word.
2. **The black spall rectangle, seven times** — listed under Q5. Two pairs sit at identical y.
3. **The 512 px verbatim repeat** at (71,70) / (583,70). Once you see it you cannot unsee that the top of the screen is one strip printed twice.
fields.Q9:
WHAT IS BEYOND THE WALLS?**
**Nothing is rendered.** Two large fields of **RGB ≈ (1, 1, 1)** — I sampled the row at y=200 from x=0 to x=310 and every value is 1. Not dark stone, not a dim room, not mass. An absence.

The boundary tells me it's a visibility cutoff and not geometry: from y=140 to y=265 the black edge sits at a hard vertical **x = 311** on the west and **x = 502** on the east; below y≈270 it curves outward (303 → 285 → 269 → 257 → 245 → 235 → 225 → 217 → 211 → 203 → 197 → 193 at y=380), which is a light circle, not a wall.

So the honest answer to "is it more of the same, empty space, or another room" is: **the image does not say.** There is no cue of any kind. The only reason I can tell the top band is remembered-but-unlit rather than distant-and-lit is that its brightness is *constant* at 7–11 across all 750 px of width, and no point light does that.
fields.Q10:
COULD YOU TELL A WAY THROUGH FROM A DEAD END?**
I found the gap: **x 377–438**, running north from y=390. Roughly 61 px wide, directly above the figure's column.

I read it as a passage — but only on second look, and for the wrong reason. It reads because it's a continuous channel that stays lit all the way to the top of the visible area, and because it lines up with the figure. It does **not** read from the structure.

Two things fight it. First, the wall ends at (377, 390) and (438, 390) are just where the slab texture stops — no return face, no jamb, no corner treatment, nothing that says "this is the end of a wall" rather than "this is where a texture ended." Second, and worse, **the passage is darker than the walls beside it**: at y=320 the corridor floor plateaus at **95** while the flanking walls sit at **114–127**. That is the inverse of the convention the eye expects. My genuine first read of that region at 1:1 was *bright slab — dark seam — bright slab*, i.e. a crack in a floor, not a corridor between two walls. Only the AO ramp at each side and the alignment with the figure corrected it.

So: passable, but you would resolve it by walking into it, not by looking at it.
fields.Q11:
HAS ANYTHING HAPPENED TO IT?**
It has been **cracked and chipped, and never touched since.**

I read that from: the crack decals (one shape, repeated); the spall decal (one shape, seven times) which shows a bevelled edge and a scatter of rubble specks below it, so a chunk came out rather than being cut out; and the complete absence of anything applied afterwards.

That is the fiction gap. The brief says a company has been repairing this line for four hundred years with rope, driven pins, hide and salvaged timber, and is extremely good at it. There is **not one repair in this image**. No pin, no lashing, no patch, no shim, no splice, no salvaged plank across anything. The wall reads as abandoned masonry in a place nobody has visited, which is close to the opposite of a held frontier. Damage without repair reads as *ruin*; damage with ugly competent repair reads as *occupied*. This is ruin.

---
fields.CULL: Wall and floor are one stone at two brightnesses; a 54×170px block repeats verbatim 512px away.
fields.FLIP LIST:
- Give the wall its own albedo — currently wall and floor sample identically at 1.00/0.71/0.45 normalized RGB, everywhere. Separate the two by value *and* hue so the corridor at x 377–438 stops reading as a dark seam between bright slabs.
- Break the literal repeat: the 54×170 block at (71,70) is pixel-identical to (583,70), and the west column reprints itself at dy=128 (crack at (320,300) == crack at (320,172)). Needs ≥3 crack variants and ≥3 spall variants with per-instance flip/offset.
- Put something on the slab faces that survives at 1:1. Between the crack squiggles the surface is a blank gradient at every distance; add joint darkening and per-slab tonal variation strong enough to read without magnification.
- Add the repairs the fiction requires — driven pins, rope lashing, timber shoring, hide patching — spanning the cracks and the seven spall holes, so the wall reads as held rather than abandoned.
- Extend the corridor's 12px contact shadow to the south face at y=422, which currently transitions in four pixels of flat keyline with no AO at all, and give the wall ends at (377,390) and (438,390) a shaped return so the opening reads as an opening.

*Model: Claude Opus 5 (1M context).*
